introduction: After the Christmas season, the Church returns to Ordinary Time with two stories of being called. The boy Samuel hears his name in the night and learns to answer, "Speak; for your servant hears." In the Gospel, two disciples of John follow Jesus, and he asks them, "What are you looking for?" His answer to their question is an invitation: "Come and see." Paul reminds us that we belong to the Lord in body as well as spirit. Let us come to this Mass ready to listen for the voice that calls each of us by name.

prayerOfTheFaithful.invitation: Brothers and sisters, the Lord calls each of us by name. With open hearts, let us answer him in prayer.
intentions: For the Church: that, like John the Baptist, she may always point beyond herself to Jesus, the Lamb of God. Let us pray to the Lord.
For young people discerning their path in life: that they may hear the Lord's call and have the courage to answer, "Here I am." Let us pray to the Lord.
For priests, deacons, religious, and all who guide others in faith: that, like Eli, they may help others recognize the voice of God. Let us pray to the Lord.
For all who feel unheard, overlooked, or alone: that they may discover that God knows them by name and has never stopped calling them. Let us pray to the Lord.
For our parish: that we may honor God in our bodies and in our daily lives, and welcome newcomers with the invitation, "Come and see." Let us pray to the Lord.
prayerOfTheFaithful.conclusion: Lord God, you called Samuel in the night and the first disciples by the Jordan. Give us listening hearts and willing feet, so that we may follow your Son wherever he leads. Through Christ our Lord.

reflection.title: Come and see
reflection.body:
Three times the voice calls Samuel, and three times he runs to the wrong person. "Samuel didn't yet know the LORD," the reading explains. It takes the old priest Eli to recognize what is happening and to teach the boy how to respond: "Speak, LORD; for your servant hears." Even a true call often needs someone else to help us hear it.

John the Baptist plays that role in the Gospel. He sees Jesus walk by and says, "Behold, the Lamb of God!" Two of his own disciples leave him to follow Jesus, and John lets them go. A good guide in faith does not keep people for himself.

Jesus turns and asks the first words he speaks in John's Gospel: "What are you looking for?" It is still his question to us. The disciples answer with another question, "where are you staying?", and Jesus does not hand them an explanation. He says, "Come and see." Faith begins as an invitation to spend time with him. They stay that day, and one of them, Andrew, runs to his brother: "We have found the Messiah!"

Paul adds that this belonging is not only spiritual. "Don't you know that your bodies are members of Christ?" he asks, and again: "your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you." Following Jesus shapes how we treat our bodies, our time, and the people around us.

This week, make room for a few minutes of silence each day and pray Samuel's words. Then think of one person you could invite, as Andrew invited Simon, to come and see.
